t-9006.author: kbrandt
t-9006.title: Ask HN: how do you interview for systems work without a whiteboard?
t-9006.body: We have replaced the algorithms round with a debugging session on a recorded failure: candidate gets a repository, a failing test and two hours. It reads better than the whiteboard and takes four times as long to prepare. For those who have run something similar for more than a year - did it survive contact with a hiring spike, and what did you cut first?

replies.author: bmartinez
replies.body: We run something close to this. What we cut first was the two hours - it became forty five minutes on a failure we had already narrowed to one file. Still better than a whiteboard, and it stopped being the reason nobody wanted to be on the loop.

replies.author: throwaway_sim
replies.body: Forty five minutes on a pre-narrowed failure is a code reading exercise with extra steps. Which is fine, but call it that.

replies.author: bmartinez
replies.body: Fair. Calling it a code reading exercise is honest and I would rather hire on code reading than on whether someone has seen this dynamic programming trick before.

replies.author: kbrandt
replies.body: Twelve minutes of elevated latency is not 'down', and a title that says otherwise is why nobody trusts the front page for incidents.

replies.author: dokoro
replies.body: SRE at Northstar. It was 12 minutes of elevated API latency, not an outage, and the timeline on the status page is the real one - we replayed the checkpoint rather than reconstructing it, which is why the minute marks are exact.

replies.author: throwaway_sim
replies.body: Appreciate the response and I will take the correction on the title.

replies.author: cnakamura
replies.body: The postmortem will be up on the engineering blog today. It is short because the reproduction did most of the work.

t-9004.author: bmartinez
t-9004.title: Hash order bit me: three weeks for a nine line fix

replies.author: praman
replies.body: This is the best written version of a bug I answer about once a quarter. The important sentence is that it passed on every machine the author owned - that is what makes it three weeks instead of an afternoon.

replies.author: kbrandt
replies.body: Every language has a version of this. Go randomised map iteration deliberately so you would find out on day one instead of in year three, and people still write code that depends on it.

t-9005.author: achen
t-9005.title: Show HN: Atlas, a simulated machine you can replay byte for byte
t-9005.body: Atlas simulates a whole machine - processes, filesystem, network and browser - from one u64 seed, and ships a harness that reruns a recorded session and compares every frame. Walkthrough: http://youtube.com/watch?v=atlas-walkthrough

replies.author: kbrandt
replies.body: What happens when a dependency you do not control calls the clock? That is where every project like this has quietly given up.

replies.author: achen
replies.body: We vendor it, patch it, or drop it, and the patches directory has a README that opens with an apology. There is no fourth option and pretending otherwise is how you end up with a replay harness that passes because it is not actually checking anything.

replies.author: praman
replies.body: The apology README is the strongest signal in this whole thread that the project is real.

replies.author: throwaway_sim
replies.body: Having tried to sell reproducibility to a team that did not want it: the hard part is not the engineering, it is that determinism removes the excuse. Some organisations are load bearing on that excuse.

t-9001.author: tomw
t-9001.title: Northstar's Atlas bets everything on determinism

replies.author: kbrandt
replies.body: The enforcement section is the only part of this that matters, and to the author's credit it is most of the article. A replay harness that fails the build is a claim you can check; everything else is a press release.

replies.author: achen
replies.body: Author of the renderer. The three week bug in the middle of the piece is accurate, including the part where I inspected the hash map early and decided it was not the problem.

replies.author: praman
replies.body: For anyone who wants the technical version rather than the profile, it is the accepted answer here: http://stackoverflow.com/questions/t-4411

replies.author: throwaway_sim
replies.body: Determinism is table stakes in a few regulated industries and nobody writes profiles about those teams, because the software is beige and the people are not quotable.

replies.author: tomw
replies.body: I would genuinely like to write that story. If you work on one of those systems and can talk on the record, my contact details are on The Verge.

replies.author: cnakamura
replies.body: The quote about incorrect parts staying still is mine and I have already been told it is going on a mug.

replies.author: kbrandt
replies.body: Keeping a known bug because fixing it correctly would break replay for everyone is the most interesting decision in this post, and it is one paragraph. I would read four thousand words on just that.

replies.author: achen
replies.body: It is a five millisecond delay on the first frame after a resize. The correct fix makes the frame clock depend on the host, which breaks every recorded session anyone has. The issue is open and the release notes say so.

replies.author: praman
replies.body: The eighteen-months-later deletion of your own abstraction is the other half of this post and nobody will quote it, because it is not flattering to anyone including the author.
